description: Grouped here are membrane proteins of the Golgi apparatus, the sorting and finishing station through which newly made proteins and lipids pass on their way to the cell surface, secretion or the endolysosomal system. Much of the chemistry that distinguishes one glycan or lipid from another happens on these membranes: a beta-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase builds lacto-series glycosphingolipid cores, and a GalNAc transferase initiates chondroitin sulfate chains on proteoglycans destined for the extracellular matrix. Alongside the biosynthetic enzymes sit cargo receptors that decide where material goes — sortilin directing traffic out of the trans-Golgi network toward endosomes, and Wntless escorting lipid-modified Wnt ligands to the surface so that developmental signalling can occur at all. Secreted growth factors, sphingolipid- and phospholipid-modifying enzymes, and receptors bound for endosomal compartments all transit this same machinery, linking Golgi membrane identity to secretion, matrix formation and intercellular signalling.

description: The mitotic cell cycle is the ordered programme by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it equally into two daughters, passing through G1, S, G2 and M; its fidelity determines whether tissues renew correctly and whether daughter cells inherit an intact, correctly counted chromosome set. Cyclin-CDK modules set the tempo, with D- and E-type cyclins releasing E2F from RB1 to license origins via the MCM helicase, CDC6 and CDT1 (restrained by geminin), and cyclin B-CDK1 driving mitotic entry under opposing control from WEE1 and the CDC25 phosphatases. In mitosis, gamma-tubulin nucleated spindles, kinetochore complexes such as NDC80, the aurora B passenger complex and the spindle assembly checkpoint govern attachment before the APC/C triggers separase-dependent cohesin cleavage; ESCRT proteins complete abscission. DNA damage checkpoints through ATM, ATR, CHK1/2 and p53 arrest progression, and loss of these brakes underlies aneuploidy and cancer.

description: T cells commit to an immune response only when their receptor engages a peptide displayed on an MHC molecule at the surface of an antigen-presenting cell, and this pathway covers the contact itself and the accessory signals that decide whether the encounter activates or restrains the cell. It underlies all adaptive cellular immunity — clearance of infected and tumour cells, help for antibody responses — and its miscalibration produces autoimmunity or immune escape. Antigen display depends on class II peptide loading machinery, while stable adhesion is built by LFA-1 (ITGAL) binding ICAM-1, with the Rap1 effector RIAM licensing integrin engagement to form the immunological synapse. Superimposed on this are modulatory receptors: the checkpoint TIM-3 with its ligand galectin-9, inhibitory MHC class I recognition by LILRB1, plexin–semaphorin contacts, and TREM2 signalling through the DAP12 adaptor in the presenting myeloid cell.

description: Amplifying T cell mediated immunity means raising the frequency and vigour with which T cells recognise antigen and act on it, the arm of adaptive defence that clears intracellular pathogens and transformed cells and that drives autoimmunity and graft rejection when it runs unchecked. Much of this happens at the antigen-presentation step: MHC class I heavy chains with beta-2 microglobulin, class II molecules, the CD1 family for lipid antigens and MR1 for microbial metabolites display ligands to conventional and unconventional T cells, with peptide loading supported by transporter machinery. Costimulatory and stress-induced surface ligands, including OX40L, nectin-family poliovirus receptor proteins and the ULBP/RAET1 NKG2D ligands, lower the threshold for activation. Inflammasome-driven IL-1beta plus IL-12, IL-18, IL-23, IL-4 and IL-6 then instruct helper lineages through T-bet and GATA3, while TCR-proximal signalling via CD45, MALT1, TAK1 and TRAF adaptors converges on NF-kB; FOXP3 marks the regulatory brake on the same circuit.

description: Arterial pressure is set moment to moment by circulating and locally released chemical mediators acting on vascular tone, renal salt and water handling, and cardiac output; this is the hormonal, autocrine and paracrine limb of blood pressure control, as opposed to neural reflexes. Its core is the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis: renin cleaves angiotensinogen, ACE generates angiotensin II for the AT1 receptor and aldosterone synthesis, while ACE2 and the receptor MAS1 form an opposing vasodilatory arm, with mast cell chymase and cathepsin G providing alternative peptide processing. Counter-regulation comes from endothelial nitric oxide synthase, natriuretic peptide maturation by corin and its degradation by neprilysin, and mineralocorticoid protection by HSD11B2, balanced against endothelins, vasopressin and adrenergic receptor signalling. Derangement of these mediators underlies essential and secondary hypertension, and they are the targets of most antihypertensive drugs.

description: This is the control layer over carbohydrate metabolism: the hormonal, kinase and transcriptional inputs that decide whether a cell stores glucose as glycogen, burns it, or makes it anew. It sets fasting and postprandial blood glucose, and its failure is the substance of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and glycogen storage disease. Insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors and AKT opposes glucagon and glucocorticoid signalling through cyclic AMP and FOXO1, while glucokinase and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase set flux at the committed steps of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. Glycogen handling is tuned by GSK3 and by the PPP1R3 family of glycogen-targeting phosphatase subunits, and pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases divert pyruvate away from oxidation. Nutrient sensors AMPK, mTORC1, sirtuins, O-GlcNAc transferase and glucose-responsive transcription factors, together with adipokines such as leptin and adiponectin, couple this to whole-body energy state.

description: Chromatin organization is the set of activities that package genomic DNA with histones and then continually rebuild, mark and reposition that packaging so that transcription, replication, repair and chromosome segregation can happen on the right sequences at the right time. It covers the core and variant histones themselves, chaperones such as ASF1A and the CAF-1 subunits that deposit nucleosomes behind the replication fork, and ATP-dependent remodellers of the SWI/SNF, CHD, INO80 and ISWI families that slide or evict them. Overlaid on this are the writers, erasers and readers of histone and DNA modification — acetyltransferases and HDACs, PRC1 and PRC2 repressive complexes, KMT and KDM enzymes, DNMTs and TET dioxygenases — plus architectural factors like CTCF and cohesin that fold the genome into loops, CENPA-based centromere assembly, and the protamine-driven repackaging of sperm. Mutations across these complexes cause developmental syndromes and are among the commonest drivers in cancer.

description: Ribosome production begins with a single long polymerase I transcript that must be cleaved, trimmed and chemically modified to yield the mature 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNAs, and rRNA processing is that conversion. Its output sets the translational capacity of the cell, which is why defects cause the ribosomopathies — bone marrow failure, skeletal and craniofacial malformation — and why cancers with high growth demand upregulate it. The work is carried out in the nucleolus by large assembly intermediates: a small-subunit processome built from UTP and WDR proteins, dozens of DEAD-box and DEAH-box helicases that remodel folding intermediates, and endo- and exonucleases including XRN2 and the multi-subunit RNA exosome that define the mature ends. Guide snoRNPs containing fibrillarin or the pseudouridine synthase DKC1 install methyl and pseudouridine marks, while late cytoplasmic steps such as SBDS-dependent release of eIF6 license the subunit for translation. A parallel set of methyltransferases and pseudouridine synthases performs the equivalent maturation of mitochondrial rRNA.

description: Proteins are made in one place and must work in another, and protein targeting is the collection of routes that read address information in a nascent chain and deliver it to the right compartment. Nothing about compartmentalized cell biology survives its failure: secretory cargo, lysosomal hydrolases, respiratory chain subunits and peroxisomal enzymes all end up mislocalized and degraded. The signal recognition particle and its ER receptor pause translation at the membrane, the Sec61 channel translocates the chain, and signal peptidase removes the address once used. Mitochondrial import runs through outer- and inner-membrane translocases with intermembrane chaperones, and presequences are trimmed by processing peptidases. Peroxisomal receptors bind PTS1 and PTS2 signals; tail-anchored proteins use a separate insertion machinery; palmitoyltransferases and mannose-6-phosphate tagging add lipid and glycan addresses. Downstream sorting complexes, ubiquitin ligases and autophagy factors route or retire what arrives. Defects underlie peroxisome biogenesis disorders and lysosomal storage disease.

description: The innermost germ layer of the gastrulating embryo gives rise to the gut tube and its derivatives \u2014 liver, pancreas, thyroid, lung and the whole gastrointestinal lining \u2014 and endoderm development covers its specification from pluripotent epiblast through to organ-forming epithelium. Nodal and other TGF-beta family ligands signal through SMAD2/SMAD3 with SMAD4 to induce transcription factors such as EOMES, MIXL1 and SOX17, while pluripotency regulators including NANOG and POU5F1 set the competence window and BMP and Wnt inputs, tuned by secreted antagonists like noggin and DKK1, position endoderm relative to mesoderm. Chromatin machinery, notably the PAF1 transcription elongation complex and histone-modifying enzymes, stabilises these fate decisions. Cells then move: integrins, laminins, collagens and matrix metalloproteinases build and remodel basement membrane during gut tube morphogenesis, and later factors such as HNF1B, ONECUT1 and NKX2-1 pattern individual organs. Disruption causes gastrulation arrest and foregut malformations.

description: Heart development covers the whole trajectory by which mesodermal progenitors become a four-chambered, rhythmically contracting pump: specification of cardiac lineages, looping of the primitive tube, septation, valve formation, outflow tract remodelling, coronary vessel growth and maturation of the conduction system. It is the biology whose failure produces congenital heart disease, the commonest class of birth defect, as well as inherited cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia. Core transcription factors such as NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, TBX20 and the HAND bHLH proteins set chamber and lineage identity, acting downstream of BMP, TGF-beta, WNT, FGF, Hedgehog and Notch signalling from surrounding tissues. Nodal, PITX2, ZIC3 and ciliary components including DNAH5 and FOXJ1 establish the left-right asymmetry the heart must follow. Endocardial-to-mesenchymal transition and matrix remodelling build the valves, while sarcomeric proteins, calcium-handling machinery, ion channels such as SCN5A and HCN4, and muscle-enriched microRNAs bring the maturing myocardium into function.

description: Behaviour is the coordinated output of the nervous system — feeding, sleep and arousal, locomotion, mating, social interaction, learning and memory, fear and reward-seeking — generated when sensory and internal signals are converted into action. The genes supporting it span the whole chain: neurotransmitter synthesis and clearance (tyrosine hydroxylase, glutamate decarboxylase, the dopamine and serotonin transporters), receptors for dopamine, serotonin, opioids, acetylcholine, glutamate and GABA, and the synaptic adhesion and scaffolding machinery (neurexins, neuroligins, SHANK proteins, CNTNAP2) that builds the circuits in which they act. Hypothalamic neuropeptide systems — leptin and its receptor, POMC and AGRP acting through melanocortin receptors, orexin, oxytocin and vasopressin — set appetite, wakefulness and social state, while clock components tie these outputs to daily time. Disruption underlies autism, intellectual disability, addiction, obesity and the behavioural decline of neurodegenerative disease.

description: Carbohydrate transport covers the movement of sugars and related polyols across membranes, the step that lets cells acquire fuel and lets the body distribute glucose between gut, blood, liver, muscle and brain. Two transporter families dominate: facilitative carriers of the GLUT class, including the ubiquitous GLUT1 and the insulin-responsive GLUT4, and sodium-coupled cotransporters such as SGLT1 and SGLT2 that drive uptake against a gradient in intestinal and renal epithelia. Aquaglyceroporins add routes for water and glycerol. Much of the accompanying machinery is regulatory rather than transport itself: insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors, PI3K and AKT triggers translocation of GLUT4-containing vesicles to the plasma membrane, while adipokines, hexokinase-mediated trapping of imported glucose, and transcriptional and microRNA inputs tune capacity. Failure at these steps produces insulin resistance, diabetes, renal glycosuria and glucose-transporter deficiency encephalopathy.

description: Wnt signalling begins when a secreted Wnt lipid-modified glycoprotein engages a Frizzled receptor with LRP5/6 co-receptors, and ends with a change in transcription that decides whether a cell proliferates, stays a stem cell, or adopts a particular fate and orientation. It patterns the embryonic axis, maintains intestinal, skin and bone stem cell compartments, and builds bone mass; its loss causes skeletal and developmental malformations, while constitutive activation through APC or beta-catenin mutation drives colorectal and other cancers. In the resting state a destruction complex of APC, Axin, GSK3 and casein kinase 1 marks beta-catenin for ubiquitin-dependent degradation; receptor activation disables it, letting beta-catenin enter the nucleus and convert TCF/LEF factors from repressors into activators of targets such as MYC and cyclin D1. Ligand availability is tuned by Porcupine and Wntless, by secreted antagonists including DKKs, SFRPs and sclerostin, and by R-spondin control of RNF43/ZNRF3-mediated receptor turnover. description: Leukotriene biosynthesis converts membrane arachidonic acid into the lipid mediators that drive bronchoconstriction, vascular leak and neutrophil recruitment, making it the pathway behind asthma, allergic inflammation and the target of anti-leukotriene drugs. A phospholipase A2 step liberates arachidonate from phospholipid, and 5-lipoxygenase, working with its membrane-anchored activating protein FLAP at the nuclear envelope, oxygenates it to the unstable epoxide LTA4. From there the route forks: a cytosolic hydrolase yields the chemoattractant LTB4, while glutathione conjugation by LTC4 synthase or related MAPEG enzymes yields LTC4, which is exported by an ATP-driven transporter and trimmed by gamma-glutamyl transferases into the cysteinyl leukotrienes acting on airway smooth muscle. Immunoreceptor tyrosine kinase signalling in mast cells, eosinophils and myeloid cells triggers the cascade, linking innate immune activation to lipid mediator output.

description: Tissues acquire their shapes through cell movement, adhesion and oriented growth, and this pathway covers the signals that tune the pace and extent of anatomical structure morphogenesis rather than initiating it. Endothelial members such as ENG, ACVRL1, KRIT1, CCM2 and PDCD10 link the same logic to blood vessel shape.

description: Beta cells of the pancreatic islet exist to release insulin in proportion to circulating nutrients, and this pathway is the machinery that couples a rise in blood glucose to granule exocytosis. Its failure, whether by loss of beta-cell identity or by defective coupling, produces hyperglycaemia and diabetes; several members are the classic monogenic diabetes genes. Glucose enters through GLUT2 and is committed by glucokinase, the flux-setting sensor; the resulting ATP closes KATP channels built from SUR1 and Kir6.2, depolarizing the cell so that voltage-gated calcium entry triggers SNARE-mediated fusion of insulin granules involving SNAP25, syntaxin-1A, RAB3A and synaptotagmin-7. description: Before a messenger RNA can leave the nucleus it must be cut at its 3' end and given a poly(A) tail, and this pathway covers the factors that stimulate that step rather than performing the cleavage themselves. Efficient 3'-end formation sets transcript stability, export competence and translatability, and determines which polyadenylation site is chosen, so its enhancement shapes mRNA isoform output and prevents readthrough transcription. The nuclear cap-binding complex, formed by CBP80 and CBP20 on the 5' m7G cap, couples the two ends of a nascent transcript and promotes cleavage and polyadenylation downstream. Paf1 complex subunit CDC73 links transcriptional elongation by RNA polymerase II to the processing machinery, while the G-quadruplex-unwinding helicase DHX36 resolves RNA structure that would otherwise obstruct processing. A mitotic cyclin ties this activity to cell cycle progression, connecting 3'-end maturation to proliferative gene expression.

description: Methylation covers the transfer of a methyl group, almost always from S-adenosylmethionine, onto DNA, RNA, proteins, lipids, small metabolites and xenobiotics, and it is one of the cell's main ways of marking molecules without changing their sequence. Its outputs range from heritable gene silencing to hormone turnover and drug clearance. DNMT1 and DNMT3A/3B methylate CpG cytosines to set imprinting and lineage-restricted silencing; histone writers such as EZH2, the KMT2, SETD, SUV39 and PRDM families, and the arginine methyltransferases PRMT1 and PRMT5, tune chromatin and transcription; METTL3 with METTL14 installs m6A on mRNA while large TRMT, NSUN and FTSJ families modify tRNA and rRNA for accurate translation. Small-molecule enzymes including COMT and TPMT inactivate catecholamines and thiopurines, while methionine synthase and a mitochondrial SAM carrier keep donor supply running. Loss of individual enzymes causes overgrowth syndromes, intellectual disability, leukaemia and altered drug toxicity.

description: Ion fluxes across membranes must be damped as well as initiated, and negative regulation of ion transmembrane transport gathers the brakes: inhibitory subunits, scaffolds, kinases, phosphatases, ubiquitin ligases and microRNAs that reduce how much current or pump activity a membrane sustains. description: The intestinal epithelium renews itself every few days, and that depends on crypt-base stem cells dividing at a rate matched exactly to the loss of differentiated cells above them. Intestinal stem cell homeostasis is the set of controls that keeps this pool at constant size: too little activity and the epithelial barrier fails to regenerate after injury, too much and crypts become hyperproliferative, a step toward adenoma formation. Lipid metabolism provides a second layer, as phospholipid acyl-chain remodelling by LPCAT3 and secreted phospholipases such as PLA2G2A alter membrane composition, signalling lipid availability and the antimicrobial output of neighbouring Paneth cells. Microbial and chromatin inputs also feed in, including NOD2 sensing of bacterial peptidoglycan, linking crypt renewal to gut flora and to inflammatory bowel disease risk.

description: Nerve terminals hold only a limited pool of synaptic vesicles, so sustained transmission depends on rebuilding them locally rather than shipping replacements from the soma. In synaptic vesicle recycling via an endosomal intermediate, membrane retrieved from the plasma membrane through clathrin-coated pits is delivered first to an endosomal compartment, where cargo is sorted before vesicles are regenerated, re-acidified by the vesicular proton pump, and reloaded with neurotransmitter. This route allows quality control over vesicle protein composition, and it overlaps with the endosomal machinery that recycles neurotransmitter receptors. Intersectins act as scaffolds coupling the clathrin machinery to actin and small GTPase regulation at the site of budding, the AP-3 adaptor complex sorts cargo out of endosomes toward vesicle formation, and RAB7A governs endosome maturation. Loss of these steps degrades release fidelity during high-frequency firing.

description: During gastrulation, epiblast cells must decide whether to become mesoderm, and this regulatory module sets how many do so and how fast, tuning mesodermal cell fate specification up or down. description: Penile erection is a vascular event under neural and endocrine control: arterial inflow into the corpus cavernosum rises, sinusoidal smooth muscle relaxes, and venous outflow is compressed, so the organ stiffens and enlarges sufficiently for intercourse. Its failure is erectile dysfunction, one of the commonest consequences of diabetes, atherosclerosis and pelvic nerve injury, while unregulated persistence of the same relaxation produces priapism. The genes here span the levels of that control. Oxytocin acts centrally from hypothalamic neurons to promote arousal and pro-erectile autonomic outflow. Endothelin and purinergic receptors sit on endothelium and cavernosal smooth muscle, where they set vasomotor tone. Adenosine deaminase clears adenosine, a potent vasodilator whose accumulation drives prolonged, unwanted engorgement, illustrating that timely reversal of relaxation matters as much as achieving it. Activin receptor signalling links the tissue to broader growth-factor control.

description: Pigmentation is the deposition of melanin in skin, hair and eye, which sets visible colouring and shields tissue from ultraviolet damage; its failure produces albinism, deafness-pigmentary syndromes and hypopigmented patches, and its cells are the origin of melanoma. The programme spans lineage specification, in which MITF, SOX10, SNAI2 and ZEB2 commit neural crest cells to the melanocyte fate while KIT with its ligand KITLG and endothelin signalling through EDNRB and EDN3 drive melanoblast migration and survival. Mature melanocytes build melanosomes, lysosome-related organelles in which tyrosinase, TYRP1 and DCT synthesise melanin from tyrosine, aided by melanosomal transporters such as OCA2 and SLC45A2 and the fibrillar matrix protein PMEL. Output is tuned by MC1R and its antagonist ASIP. Cargo delivery uses AP-3 and BLOC complexes, and RAB27A with MYO5A and MLPH tethers melanosomes for transfer to keratinocytes.

description: Hearing depends on a small, non-renewable population of auditory hair cells in the cochlea, and this pathway sets how many of them form and when. It governs the balance between hair cells and the supporting cells that surround them within the sensory epithelium, so that too little or too much differentiation leaves an organ of Corti that cannot transduce sound; loss of these cells in humans is irreversible and underlies sensorineural deafness. The core logic is lateral inhibition: the proneural factor ATOH1 commits a progenitor to hair cell fate, while a Delta-like ligand activates NOTCH1 on neighbours, inducing HES and HEY family repressors that shut ATOH1 expression down and hold those cells as supporting cells. MYC-family factors contribute proliferative capacity in the prosensory domain, and RNA-level control through the splicing regulator ESRP1 shapes the epithelial programme, mutations in which cause hearing loss.

description: Cells scale up fatty acid synthesis when nutrients are plentiful, and this is the regulatory input that pushes lipogenesis upward rather than the biosynthetic chemistry itself. It matters for hepatic and adipose fat storage, milk and sebum production, membrane expansion in growing cells, and, when overactive, for hepatic steatosis, hypertriglyceridaemia and the lipid phenotype of metabolic syndrome. Control is largely transcriptional: the glucose-responsive factor ChREBP and the oxysterol-sensing liver X receptors turn on lipogenic gene programmes, with acetylation-modifying enzymes and microRNAs tuning the output. Other members act post-transcriptionally or on substrate supply — MID1IP1 promotes activation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, ELOVL5 extends the chains produced, and apolipoprotein activators of lipoprotein lipase together with its endothelial anchor deliver fatty acids from circulating triglyceride. Inflammatory and hormonal signals, including interleukin-1β, endothelins and vasopressin, feed into the same set point.

description: Paraxial mesoderm morphogenesis shapes the bands of mesoderm flanking the neural tube into segmented somites, the source of skeletal muscle, vertebrae, ribs and dermis; when it fails, the axial skeleton is malformed or fused and segment number and identity are lost. Wnt ligands supply both arms of the input: WNT3A sustains posterior progenitors and, with LEF1 as the nuclear effector of beta-catenin, drives paraxial fate, while WNT5A and WNT11 act through planar-polarity routes that orient cells for convergent extension. BMP signalling through the type I receptor BMPR1A sets dorsoventral position, and SMAD2 and SMAD3 relay activin/Nodal-family cues that pattern the mesoderm. The forkhead factors FOXC1 and FOXC2 act largely redundantly to permit somite formation and sclerotome differentiation. Cell-shape change and directed migration require membrane traffic and branched actin assembly, contributed here by exocyst and WAVE-complex components.

description: Sour taste reports acidity, warning against spoiled or unripe food and contributing, with salt sensing, to how animals judge what is safe to swallow. This pathway covers the detection of protons at the apical surface of taste receptor cells, the conversion of that chemical stimulus into membrane depolarization, and its relay to gustatory afferent fibres. Most of the participants belong to the degenerin/epithelial sodium channel family: acid-sensing channels open directly in response to extracellular acidification and carry inward sodium current, while the epithelial sodium channel subunits form the amiloride-sensitive conductance long studied in taste epithelium. A distinct transient receptor potential polycystin channel and its polycystin-1-like partner mark the type III taste cells that respond to acids and have been proposed to contribute to their acid response. Loss of this sensing blunts avoidance of acidic and potentially harmful foods.

description: Vascular and visceral smooth muscle cells are not terminally locked in: they toggle between a contractile state and a proliferative, synthetic, migratory one, and the processes gathered here are those that hold back or reverse contractile differentiation. This plasticity is what allows vessels to remodel and wounds to heal, and its excess is what drives neointima formation after angioplasty, atherosclerotic plaque growth and hypertensive vessel stiffening. Mitogenic and morphogenic ligands such as PDGF-B, FGF9, epiregulin and hedgehog signal cells away from the contractile programme; Notch-induced repressors HEY1 and HEY2, the Mediator subunit MED28 and the PR-domain factor PRDM6 block differentiation transcriptionally, while DNMT1 and the methyl-CpG reader MECP2 impose epigenetic silencing. Calcineurin-NFAT signalling, tuned by its inhibitor RCAN1, adds a calcium-responsive input, and a set of microRNAs together with RNA-binding and translational regulators enforces the same suppression after transcription.

description: Before a cell divides, every chromosome must be captured by microtubules from opposite spindle poles, and regulating the attachment of spindle microtubules to kinetochores is how correct captures are stabilized and incorrect ones destroyed. Getting this wrong produces lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and the chromosomal instability typical of tumours, so the same machinery also enforces the delay in anaphase onset until biorientation is achieved. Central to it is the chromosomal passenger complex, in which Aurora B kinase, bound to INCENP with survivin and borealin, phosphorylates outer-kinetochore substrates to release attachments that lack tension. Counterbalancing factors include the astrin–kinastrin pair, which marks stably bioriented kinetochores, and the RZZ components ZW10, ZWILCH and KNTC1, which build the checkpoint-signalling platform. Mitotic CDK1–cyclin B activity, NEK2, and acetylation and deacetylation by lysine acetyltransferases and sirtuins tune the process across mitosis into cytokinesis.

description: Most of the skeleton is not built directly as bone but first modelled in cartilage, and endochondral bone morphogenesis is the conversion of that cartilage template into mineralized bone. It sets limb and vertebral length, drives postnatal growth at the growth plate, and its disturbance produces the skeletal dysplasias — short-limbed dwarfism, brittle or undermineralized bone, premature growth plate closure. Chondrocytes are specified by SOX9 and lay down a matrix of collagen II, aggrecan-type proteoglycans and matrilin; they then proliferate in columns, hypertrophy, and are replaced by RUNX2-dependent osteoblasts depositing collagen I. Pacing of that sequence depends on Indian hedgehog, BMP and TGF-beta receptor signalling, FGFR3 as a brake on proliferation, and natriuretic peptide signalling through NPR2 as an accelerator. Matrix metalloproteinases clear cartilage at the ossification front while alkaline phosphatase permits mineral deposition, coupling with vascular invasion and marrow formation.

description: Epithelial cell proliferation during salivary gland morphogenesis is the growth step that turns a simple epithelial bud into the branched, secretory architecture of the submandibular gland, expanding the cell population while shaping ducts and end buds. Without it the gland is hypoplastic or absent, with lasting consequences for saliva production, oral lubrication and mucosal defence. The core input is reciprocal signalling with the surrounding mesenchyme: FGF10 secreted by mesenchymal cells engages epithelial FGFR2, driving cell-cycle entry and bud outgrowth, while the Hedgehog ligand SHH acts as an additional morphogen coordinating branching. The homeodomain transcription factor NKX3-1 marks and regulates glandular epithelium, linking proliferation to ductal differentiation, and TNF-family cytokine signalling can modulate epithelial growth. This is a classic example of branching morphogenesis, in which proliferation, patterning and cell fate are controlled by the same ligand-receptor exchanges.

description: Coronary vasculature morphogenesis builds the arteries, capillaries and veins that perfuse the heart muscle itself, a network without which the developing myocardium cannot grow beyond a few cell layers thick and the adult heart has no reserve against ischaemia; defective coronary patterning underlies congenital coronary anomalies and shapes the myocardium's vulnerability to infarction. Endothelial progenitors derived largely from the epicardium and sinus venosus migrate into the myocardial wall, sprout under VEGFA acting through its receptors and the co-receptor NRP1, and are then stabilised by pericytes and smooth muscle recruited via PDGFRB. Notch signalling with its repressor target HEY2 imposes arterial versus venous identity, TGF-beta receptors including the co-receptor TGFBR3 license epicardial cell invasion, and cardiac transcription factors such as TBX5, TBX1 and HAND2 set the regional cues, with chromatin remodelling and Ras/MAPK restraint tuning the response.

description: Follicle-stimulating hormone from the pituitary acts on granulosa cells of the ovarian follicle and Sertoli cells of the testis, and the cellular response to that stimulus is what drives follicle growth, oocyte competence and spermatogenic support. The hormone binds FSHR, a G protein-coupled receptor that raises cAMP and reprogrammes transcription; the readouts collected here span steroidogenic capacity, redox buffering, local signalling and feedback. POR supplies electrons to the microsomal cytochrome P450 enzymes of oestrogen synthesis, while GCLC and GCLM form glutamate-cysteine ligase and set the rate of glutathione production, protecting the follicle from oxidative damage. INHBA contributes an inhibin/activin subunit that closes the loop back on pituitary FSH output. Endothelin-1 with its EDNRA receptor, Notch and ephrin-Eph signalling then act locally on vascular tone, cell fate and boundary formation within the growing follicle. Loss of this response causes hypogonadism and infertility.

description: Secreted growth factors would diffuse away or act at the wrong place if nothing held them; this is the biology that keeps proteins anchored where they belong in the extracellular region, converting the matrix into a reservoir and a positional cue. Fibrillin microfibrils provide the scaffold, and latent TGF-beta binding protein 1 tethers the small latent TGF-beta complex to it, so that ligand is stored in inactive form until mechanical or proteolytic cues release it; NRROS performs the analogous docking of latent TGF-beta1 at the cell surface. DAN-family antagonists including CER1, DAND5 and NBL1 restrain BMP and Nodal signalling by binding the ligands in the extracellular space, shaping the gradients that pattern the embryonic axis. Loss of this restraint underlies connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and dysregulated TGF-beta activation.

description: Macrophages are long-lived tissue phagocytes, and their programmed death sets how long an inflammatory or antimicrobial response persists; regulated apoptosis in these cells resolves inflammation, limits granuloma and foam-cell accumulation in infection and atherosclerosis, and disposes of cells whose lysosomes or endoplasmic reticulum have been overwhelmed. The genes here act as the survival-versus-death inputs rather than the core executioner machinery: a chemokine and its receptor provide autocrine survival signalling, innate immune sensing through a cytosolic bacterial peptidoglycan receptor and the interferon-inducing transcription factors couples pathogen detection to death decisions, a lysosomal cysteine protease and an endoplasmic reticulum selenoprotein tie organelle stress to the outcome, and a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor locus, a transcription factor and a let-7 family microRNA tune the threshold. Loss of this control leaves persistent, tissue-damaging macrophage populations or premature loss of host defence.

description: Bone resorption is carried out by giant multinucleated cells, and osteoclast fusion is the step that makes them: mononuclear precursors of the monocyte-macrophage lineage merge their plasma membranes to build a cell with many nuclei, a broad sealing zone and the ruffled border needed to dissolve mineral and degrade collagen. Without it, precursors remain mononuclear and resorption is weak, so bone accumulates and remodelling, tooth eruption and marrow cavity formation are impaired; excessive fusion accompanies the bone loss of osteoporosis, inflammatory arthritis and skeletal metastasis. Fusion depends on dedicated membrane proteins, notably the transmembrane protein DC-STAMP and the tetraspanin CD81, which organize contact sites between apposed precursors, together with TCTA. Actin remodelling through the podosome scaffold TKS5 brings membranes into apposition, while transcriptional regulators tune how readily differentiating precursors coalesce.

description: Heart rate is set by the pace at which specialized conduction tissue fires and propagates electrical impulses, and this pathway covers the ion channels and junctional proteins that tune that frequency. Pacemaker depolarization in the sinoatrial node depends on hyperpolarization-activated channels of the HCN family together with L- and T-type calcium channels such as Cav1.3 and Cav3.1, while the cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5 drives rapid conduction through working myocardium. Repolarizing potassium currents through KCNQ1 with its KCNE partners, KCNH2 and Kir2.1 determine cycle length, and acetylcholine-gated GIRK channels let vagal input slow the rate. Gap junction connexin 40, desmosomal proteins including plakophilin-2 and desmoplakin, and the adaptor ankyrin-B provide the coupling and membrane organization the impulse requires. Mutations here cause long QT and Brugada syndromes, sick sinus syndrome, atrial fibrillation and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

description: Before a cell divides, every chromosome must be captured by microtubules from both poles and brought to a plane midway between them; regulation of metaphase plate congression covers the inputs that set how fast and how completely that alignment happens. Getting it right is what makes chromosome segregation accurate, and slippage produces lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and the genomic instability characteristic of tumours. The chromosomal passenger complex, in which Aurora B kinase acts with INCENP, survivin and borealin, destabilises incorrect kinetochore attachments so biorientation can be reattempted, while astrin marks and stabilises correctly attached pairs and MAD1L1 keeps the spindle checkpoint active until congression is finished. Dynein with NUMA1 supplies poleward force and pole focusing, CDK1 sets the mitotic state, and tubulin tyrosination together with acetyltransferase and sirtuin activity tunes the microtubule and chromatin substrates involved.

description: Excitatory synapses work only if NMDA-type glutamate receptors are concentrated opposite the presynaptic release site rather than scattered over the dendritic membrane, and this clustering is what converts glutamate release into the calcium signal that drives synaptic plasticity, learning and activity-dependent circuit refinement. Trans-synaptic adhesion supplies the positional information: presynaptic neurexin binding to postsynaptic neuroligin aligns the two halves of the synapse and recruits postsynaptic density components, where large scaffolding proteins such as SHANK3 anchor receptor complexes to the actin cytoskeleton. Secreted reelin, acting through lipoprotein receptors of the LDL receptor family, tunes receptor subunit composition and positioning during maturation, a route in which apolipoprotein E also participates. Disruption of these components is repeatedly implicated in autism, intellectual disability, schizophrenia and neurodegeneration, linking receptor placement to cognition.

description: Every heartbeat begins with a stereotyped electrical waveform, and regulation of the cardiac muscle cell action potential is the tuning of that waveform's shape, duration and propagation from cell to cell. It sets heart rate, coordinates atrial and ventricular contraction, and when disturbed produces long-QT and Brugada syndromes, conduction block, sick sinus syndrome and lethal ventricular arrhythmia. Depolarizing and pacemaker currents are carried by the L-type calcium channel Cav1.2 and the hyperpolarization-activated HCN channels of the sinoatrial node, while calcium released through RyR2 and resequestered by SERCA2 couples excitation to contraction and feeds back on the channels themselves through calmodulin and CaMKII. Adaptor and scaffolding proteins such as ankyrin-B, caveolin-3, AKAP9 and BIN1 position channels in the correct membrane microdomain, and connexins with desmosomal proteins of the intercalated disc pass the impulse between myocytes.

description: Removing the 5' cap commits a messenger RNA to destruction, and RNA decapping is the irreversible step that ends a transcript's life and thereby sets how long any protein continues to be made. It is how cells shut off inflammatory and growth-factor messages after a stimulus passes, clear defective transcripts, and hold translationally silenced mRNAs in cytoplasmic P-bodies. Shortening of the poly(A) tail by the CCR4-NOT and PAN2-PAN3 deadenylases comes first; the LSM1-7 ring recognises the shortened tail and, with scaffolds such as PATL1, EDC3 and EDC4 and the helicase DDX6, delivers the transcript to the DCP2 holoenzyme with its DCP1 activators. The exposed 5' monophosphate end is then chewed away by the exonuclease XRN1. Related Nudix and related hydrolases handle other cap species, including leftover cap dinucleotides and non-canonical NAD caps, while ARE-binding factors like ZFP36 select which messages enter the route.

description: Cytosolic double-stranded DNA, whether from an invading pathogen or a damaged nucleus, is read as a danger signal by the AIM2 inflammasome, and this regulatory layer sets how readily that complex is allowed to form. Assembly nucleates ASC into a speck that activates caspase-1, releasing IL-1β and IL-18 and driving pyroptotic death, so the threshold matters: too little and intracellular bacteria and viruses escape control, too much and self-DNA provokes autoinflammatory tissue damage. Interferon-inducible guanylate-binding GTPases such as GBP2 and GBP5 act on the permissive side, helping expose microbial DNA to the sensor, while the pyrin-domain-only protein PYDC5 works as a decoy that blocks productive PYD–PYD contacts and the E3 ligase TRIM11 restrains signalling by targeting the sensor for disposal. IFI16, a related nuclear and cytosolic DNA sensor, shapes the same response.

description: Not every amino acid a cell makes ends up in protein. This route generates the non-proteinogenic amino acids that serve as neurotransmitters, urea-cycle intermediates, structural modifications and metabolic carriers, and its outputs shape inhibitory neurotransmission, nitrogen disposal and connective tissue strength. Glutamate decarboxylases produce GABA, the principal inhibitory transmitter, which a transaminase later returns to the TCA cycle; serine racemase converts L-serine to D-serine, the co-agonist that licenses NMDA receptor activation. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase and ornithine transcarbamylase build citrulline and ornithine for ureagenesis, with a semialdehyde synthase feeding ornithine and proline from glutamate, while pyrimidine breakdown supplies beta-alanine. Collagen lysyl hydroxylases create hydroxylysine residues required for crosslinking. Amino acid transporters keep the glutamate and glutamine precursor pools supplied. Loss of individual steps produces hyperammonaemia, epilepsy or brittle connective tissue.

description: Lactone metabolism covers the making, opening and disposal of cyclic esters, a chemistry that matters most for two things in humans: handling vitamin C, whose ascorbate ring is itself a lactone, and destroying reactive lactones and thiolactones before they damage proteins. The paraoxonase enzymes carry out the hydrolytic arm, opening lactone rings on substrates ranging from homocysteine thiolactone to bacterial acyl-homoserine lactone signals and lactone-form drugs; the HDL-associated member of this family is studied for its link to oxidised lipids and atherosclerosis risk. The transport arm brings the vitamin into cells, with sodium-coupled carriers importing reduced ascorbate and glucose transporters taking up its oxidised form, which is then recycled by glutathione-dependent reduction supported by glutamate-cysteine ligase and omega-class glutathione transferases. Endoplasmic reticulum redox proteins tie the pathway to thiol-disulfide balance, placing this biology within antioxidant defence and xenobiotic detoxification.

description: When DNA damage is too severe to repair, p53 drives the cell to kill itself through the mitochondrial route, and this collection of modulators sets how readily that decision is made. Tuning it decides whether a damaged cell arrests and repairs, survives with mutations, or dies — the balance that underlies tumour suppression and much of the variation in how tumours respond to radiation and genotoxic chemotherapy. Control is exerted at several levels: translation of p53 message itself is enhanced by a ribosomal protein that binds its transcript; coactivators and chromatin-associated cofactors, together with acetylation and its removal by a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, shift p53 between arrest and apoptotic target genes; and downstream brakes act at the mitochondrion, where an antiapoptotic BCL2 family member restrains pore formation and a p53-induced factor blocks apoptosome assembly. Secreted and receptor-linked inhibitors add further damping.

description: Excitatory transmission depends not just on releasing glutamate but on tuning how much is released and when, and this regulatory layer sets the gain of glutamatergic synapses. Its components act at several points: Munc18-1 primes synaptic vesicles for SNARE-mediated fusion and its loss causes early infantile epileptic encephalopathy; the catalytic subunit of the Rab3 GTPase-activating protein switches off vesicular Rab3 to allow orderly cycles of exocytosis, with mutations producing Warburg Micro syndrome; dysbindin-1, a BLOC-1 subunit and long-standing schizophrenia candidate, modulates presynaptic release probability. Supply and receptor tone are regulated too — a sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporter imports glutamine as precursor, while kynurenine 3-monooxygenase diverts tryptophan metabolism away from kynurenic acid, an endogenous antagonist at glutamate receptors. Together these link vesicle trafficking, metabolite supply and neuromodulation to excitatory drive, seizure threshold and psychiatric risk.

description: When tissue is injured, resident fibroblasts activate, deposit matrix and contract the wound; the regulation of connective tissue replacement is the set of controls that sets how much of this scarring occurs. Getting the balance right determines whether a heart, lung, liver or kidney heals with functional tissue or with stiff fibrotic scar, and persistent overshoot underlies cardiac fibrosis, pulmonary fibrosis and cirrhosis. Control is exerted at several levels: a ligand-sensing surface receptor for advanced glycation end products and damage-associated proteins links metabolic and injury cues to fibroblast activation, Rho-activated kinases translate mechanical tension into actomyosin contractility and myofibroblast behaviour, and calcineurin-mediated dephosphorylation couples calcium signals to transcriptional responses. Nuclear receptor and transcription factor inputs, together with a large complement of microRNAs, tune the output post-transcriptionally, making this an integration point between wound healing, mechanotransduction and matrix remodelling.

description: When oxygen falls too low for a cell to sustain oxidative metabolism, the mitochondrial arm of the death programme can be engaged, and this hypoxia-triggered intrinsic apoptotic route is the decision point between adaptation and self-destruction. It matters in ischaemic tissue injury, where neurons and cardiomyocytes die after oxygen deprivation, and in tumours, where hypoxic cells that resist it survive in poorly perfused regions. Oxygen-sensitive transcription drives glycolytic and chaperone responses alongside the BH3-only protein BNIP3, which permeabilises mitochondria and also marks damaged ones for mitophagy. Opposing it are survival inputs: PI3K and MEK1-dependent kinase signalling, the caspase-inhibitory protein ARC, and Bax inhibitor-1 acting at the endoplasmic reticulum on calcium handling, while PINK1 supports mitochondrial quality control. The balance of these determines whether execution caspases are activated.

description: Potassium import across the plasma membrane is how cells build and defend the steep inward potassium gradient that sets resting membrane potential, drives secondary active transport, and lets excitable tissues repolarize. The Na+/K+-ATPase does most of the work, pumping two potassium ions in for every three sodium ions out at the cost of ATP, with beta subunits and small FXYD proteins tuning its ion affinity in a tissue-specific way; related H+/K+-ATPases take up potassium as they acidify the stomach. Inward-rectifier channels, including the ATP-sensitive pore and sulfonylurea receptor pair that couples metabolism to insulin release and vascular tone, carry potassium inward electrically, while cation-chloride cotransporters such as the renal Na-K-2Cl carrier, activated by SPAK kinase signalling, move it with sodium and chloride. Failures cause periodic paralysis, cardiac arrhythmia, salt-wasting tubulopathies and disordered insulin secretion.

description: CXCL1 is a neutrophil-attracting chemokine, and the events that increase its production set how quickly granulocytes are recruited into infected or injured tissue. Enhanced CXCL1 output drives the acute neutrophilic infiltrate of mucosal antifungal and antibacterial defence, and when sustained it contributes to psoriatic skin inflammation, arthritis and airway disease. The main input here is the IL-17 axis: IL-17A and IL-17F, secreted by Th17 and related innate lymphoid cells, engage receptor complexes containing IL-17RA on epithelial cells, fibroblasts and synoviocytes and drive NF-kB- and MAPK-dependent transcription plus stabilisation of chemokine mRNA. Innate sensing adds to this through the TIR-domain adaptor TIRAP, which relays Toll-like receptor signals to the same transcriptional output, while the calcium-permeable channel TRPV4 links mechanical and osmotic stress to inflammatory chemokine release. Together these represent adaptive, microbial and physical triggers converging on one recruitment signal.

description: Cytotoxic CD8-positive alpha-beta T cells kill infected and transformed cells, and the restraints that damp their activation set the threshold between protective immunity and autoimmune or immunopathological damage. This negative regulation keeps resting cells quiescent, limits the size of effector responses, and enforces peripheral tolerance; tumours exploit it to escape killing, which is why several of these molecules are the targets of checkpoint blockade. Inhibition acts at multiple levels: PD-L1 and VISTA are surface ligands that deliver co-inhibitory signals to responding T cells, LILRB1 is an ITIM-bearing receptor that reads MHC class I to suppress activation, and SOCS1 curbs JAK/STAT output from the cytokine receptors that drive clonal expansion. Transcriptional control also contributes, as ThPOK enforces the CD4 helper program and represses the cytotoxic alternative, with additional MHC class I-like and ion-transport proteins shaping the response.

description: Type I interferon alarms neighbouring cells before a virus reaches them, and the interferon alpha response is the transcriptional programme that alarm switches on. Its output makes a cell hostile to viral replication and visible to the immune system; loss of it leaves severe viral susceptibility, while chronic activation drives interferonopathies and contributes to lupus and other autoimmune disease. Ligand-bound receptor signals through the ISGF3 complex, with STAT2 and IRF9 binding interferon-stimulated response elements and IRF7 amplifying the loop. The induced effectors act at many steps: IFITM proteins block viral entry, PKR and the OAS-RNase L system shut down translation and degrade RNA, MX1 and viperin target replication, and tetherin holds virions at the surface. In parallel, immunoproteasome subunits, TAP1 and MHC class I components boost antigen presentation, chemokines recruit lymphocytes, and ISG15 conjugation, reversed by USP18, both marks targets and restrains the response.

description: HIV-1 depends entirely on the host RNA polymerase II machinery to express its integrated provirus, and this transcription step is the switch between latency and productive infection. Cellular factors bind cis-acting elements in the 5' long terminal repeat: TBP with its TAF partners recognises the core promoter, the general factors TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF and the TFIIH helicase/kinase module assemble a pre-initiation complex, and CDK7 phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain to launch initiation. Newly initiated polymerase is held in a promoter-proximal paused state by NELF and DSIF; the viral Tat protein overcomes this by recruiting the CDK9-cyclin T1 kinase to the TAR stem-loop, converting paused complexes into processive elongation supported by FACT and elongation factors. Nascent transcripts are capped and bound by the nuclear cap-binding complex before splicing and Rev-dependent export. Blocking this step is the basis of transcriptional latency and of efforts to silence or purge the reservoir.

description: Growth-factor signalling through the ERK cascade must be switched off as well as on, and ERK inactivation is the arm that does it, setting how long and how strongly a stimulus is read. Because ERK output controls proliferation, differentiation and survival decisions, loss of this braking step converts transient signals into sustained ones and contributes to transformation; conversely, several of the phosphatases involved are themselves induced by ERK and act as a negative feedback loop. Removal of phosphate from the threonine and tyrosine of the ERK activation loop abolishes activity: dual-specificity phosphatases such as DUSP6 and DUSP7 act largely in the cytoplasm, DUSP4 and DUSP3 in the nucleus, while the PP2A holoenzyme, built from catalytic, scaffolding and B56-type regulatory subunits, provides serine/threonine-directed dephosphorylation. ERK1, ERK2 and ERK5 are the targets, and their spatial confinement is a direct consequence of where each phosphatase resides.

description: Pancreatic islets arise from a transient population of progenitors that switch on the bHLH factor neurogenin 3, and the transcriptional programme downstream of that switch is what commits these cells to an endocrine rather than acinar or ductal fate. description: Abnormal conversion of 2-oxoglutarate to 2-hydroxyglutarate is the gain of a new catalytic activity by a mutated metabolic enzyme, and it is one of the clearest examples of metabolism itself driving cancer. Wild-type IDH1 works in the cytosol, oxidising isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate while reducing NADP+ to NADPH. Substitution of arginine 132, found recurrently in gliomas and in other tumours, reshapes the active site so the enzyme instead consumes NADPH to reduce 2-oxoglutarate to the D enantiomer of 2-hydroxyglutarate. This oncometabolite accumulates to millimolar levels and competes with 2-oxoglutarate at the many dioxygenases that require it, including DNA and histone demethylases, so chromatin and DNA methylation marks build up and differentiation stalls. Reduced NADPH availability also strains cytosolic antioxidant and reductive biosynthetic capacity, and the mutant enzyme is a direct drug target.

description: Every round of protein synthesis requires that each tRNA be loaded with its matching amino acid, and cytosolic tRNA aminoacylation is the step that establishes the correspondence between codon and amino acid on which the fidelity of translation rests. A family of class I and class II synthetases activates each amino acid with ATP and transfers it to the 3' end of tRNAs transcribed from the nuclear genome, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate, the latter hydrolysed by inorganic pyrophosphatase to keep the reaction favourable. Mutations in these enzymes, notably glycyl- and alanyl-tRNA synthetases, cause peripheral neuropathies and multisystem developmental disease.

description: Dolichyl phosphate is the lipid carrier on which nearly all glycans destined for secreted and membrane proteins are built, and dolichol kinase makes it by phosphorylating dolichol at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane using CTP. Because the defect sits at the entry point to carrier lipid production rather than at a single glycosyltransferase, it illustrates how one lipid metabolic step constrains protein glycosylation, membrane anchoring and quality control throughout the secretory pathway.

description: Death receptor engagement does not commit a cell to a single fate: when caspase-8 activity is inhibited, signalling that would have produced apoptosis is rerouted into RIPK1-dependent regulated necrosis. description: Cystic fibrosis arises when the CFTR chloride channel fails to reach the epithelial surface, and this pathway describes the quality-control machinery that destroys defective CFTR before it can get there. description: Pulmonary surfactant lowers surface tension at the alveolar air-liquid interface so that lungs can inflate at birth, and its lipid cargo must first be loaded into lamellar bodies inside alveolar type II cells. The result is pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 3, a usually fatal neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, with milder alleles presenting as childhood interstitial lung disease. description: The mitotic cell cycle is the ordered programme by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it equally into two daughters, and it underlies all tissue growth, renewal and repair; its deregulation is the defining feature of cancer, while checkpoint failure produces aneuploidy. Cyclin-dependent kinases paired with D, E, A and B cyclins set the tempo, with CDC25 phosphatases activating CDK1 and WEE1 and PKMYT1 restraining it, and CDK inhibitors such as CDKN1A imposing arrest. Retinoblastoma-family proteins and DREAM components including LIN9 and LIN54 keep E2F targets off in quiescence. Origin licensing through ORC, CDC6, CDT1 and the MCM helicase, restrained by geminin, confines replication to one round per cycle. description: Transfer RNAs are made as longer precursors and must be trimmed, spliced, tagged and chemically decorated before they can deliver amino acids to the ribosome, and tRNA processing covers that whole maturation route in both the nucleus and the mitochondrion. description: Ribosomes are built from RNA that must be cut, trimmed and chemically decorated before it can fold into a working subunit, and rRNA processing is that maturation step. description: Adenosine-to-inosine conversion is the most common form of RNA editing in humans: a deaminase acts on double-stranded regions of pre-mRNA, and because the translation machinery reads inosine as guanosine, the change can recode codons, alter splicing, or retune untranslated regions. ADAR and ADARB1 carry this out through paired double-stranded RNA-binding domains and a catalytic deaminase domain, recognising structure rather than sequence, often with help from intronic complementary sequences. Beyond recoding, such editing marks endogenous duplex RNA as self, preventing inappropriate interferon activation; its loss causes neurological and autoinflammatory disease.

description: Collagen chain trimerization is the selection step that decides which three procollagen chains will make a given collagen molecule. Before any triple helix exists, C-terminal propeptides recognise one another, enforce chain composition and stoichiometry — two alpha-1 with one alpha-2 in type I collagen, homotrimers in type III — and bring the chains into correct register so that helix formation can nucleate at the C-terminus and zipper towards the N-terminus. In type III collagen, interchain disulfide bonds lock the assembly permanently. Because it sets composition, this event determines whether fibril-forming, network-forming, anchoring, transmembrane and beaded-filament collagens are built correctly, and thereby the tensile strength of skin, bone, cartilage, basement membranes and muscle. Propeptide mutations that block correct recognition cause chains to misassemble and be retained intracellularly, producing brittle bone, chondrodysplasias, blistering skin disease and progressive kidney failure.

description: Rather than build every nucleotide from scratch, cells recover the nucleosides and free bases released by RNA and DNA turnover and re-phosphorylate them, an energetically cheap route that keeps nucleotide pools balanced and feeds interconversion and biosynthesis. Phosphoribosyltransferases return hypoxanthine, guanine and adenine to IMP, GMP and AMP; nucleoside kinases act on deoxycytidine, deoxyguanosine, thymidine and uridine, with separate cytosolic and mitochondrial kinases supplying precursors for nuclear and mitochondrial DNA replication. Deaminases and phosphorylases run the catabolic side, converting adenosine, cytidine and nucleosides to bases for reuse or disposal. The stakes are visible in disease: loss of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase causes gout with severe neurological disturbance, adenosine deaminase deficiency destroys lymphocyte development, and failure of the mitochondrial deoxyribonucleoside kinases or thymidine phosphorylase depletes mitochondrial DNA. Deoxyribonucleotide salvage normally runs at low flux, matching limited DNA turnover.

description: Inflammation does not simply fade out; it is actively switched off by lipid mediators made from omega-3 fatty acids, and this route generates that class of signals from the omega-3 docosapentaenoic acid DPAn-3. The resulting mediators limit neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of debris and apoptotic cells, and encourage tissue repair, so their availability shapes whether inflammation resolves or becomes chronic.

description: Meiotic recombination exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes, producing the genetic diversity of gametes and the physical links that let homologs segregate correctly at the first meiotic division. Without at least one crossover per bivalent, chromosomes missegregate, giving aneuploid eggs and sperm, infertility and pregnancy loss. The process begins when SPO11 cuts DNA at hotspots specified by the histone methyltransferase PRDM9; the MRN nuclease complex with CtIP removes SPO11 and resects the ends, and the exposed 3' single strands, coated by RPA and then loaded with RAD51 and the meiosis-specific recombinase DMC1 with help from BRCA2 and the HOP2–MND1 heterodimer, invade the homolog. Most joint molecules are dissolved without exchange by the BLM–TOP3A helicase route, while MSH4–MSH5 and MLH1–MLH3 channel a minority into crossovers. ATM signalling through phosphorylated H2AX, and FIGNL1:FIRRM control of recombinase dynamics, restrain break and crossover numbers within a chromatin context set by histones.

description: Oxidative attack on guanine and thymine leaves lesions that stall replication, and base excision repair normally clips them out; loss of NEIL3 function defines a defective form of that repair. NEIL3 is a DNA N-glycosylase with an unusual preference for single-stranded and quadruplex-prone DNA, excising further-oxidized guanine products such as guanidinohydantoin and spiroiminodihydantoin as well as thymine glycol, and it also unhooks certain DNA interstrand crosslinks at replication forks without help from the Fanconi anemia pathway. Its activity matters most in dividing cells: telomeres accumulate damage and shorten when it is depleted, and neural stem cells proliferate poorly and senesce early. A glycosylase-dead variant is linked to autoimmune disease, while altered expression accompanies myocardial infarction and atherosclerotic plaque growth, tying this repair activity to genome maintenance in proliferating and stressed tissues.

description: Internal tandem duplication of FLT3 is one of the most common driver lesions in acute myeloid leukaemia, and the constitutively active receptor it produces engages STAT5 far more strongly than the ligand-stimulated wild-type kinase or kinase-domain point mutants. This preferential STAT5 activation is much of what makes the mutant transforming: it converts a growth factor receptor for haematopoietic progenitors into a self-sustaining proliferation and survival signal. Autophosphorylated FLT3 recruits adaptor and scaffold proteins such as GRB2 and GAB2 together with the phosphatase SHP2, and STAT5A and STAT5B are tyrosine phosphorylated, dimerize and move to the nucleus. There they drive transcription of survival and cell cycle genes, including the anti-apoptotic Bcl-xL and the kinase PIM1, alongside regulators such as p21; NADPH oxidase-derived reactive oxygen species reinforce the signal. The axis underlies resistance to differentiation and is a target of FLT3 inhibitor therapy.

description: RHOBTB3 looks like a small GTPase but hydrolyses ATP rather than GTP, and its ATPase cycle powers membrane traffic and protein degradation rather than classical Rho-type actin signalling. The protein is prenylated and peripherally membrane-associated, and its nucleotide cycle is coupled to retrograde delivery of cargo from late endosomes back to the Golgi, working alongside RAB9A and RAB9B and endosomal sorting machinery such as HGS and PLIN3. Through its tandem BTB domains RHOBTB3 also serves as a substrate adaptor for cullin-3 ubiquitin ligase complexes, linking it to turnover of cell cycle regulators including cyclin E1 and to the hypoxia response controlled by VHL-dependent degradation. Loss of this activity slows endosome-to-Golgi return and relieves degradative control of proliferation drivers; RHOBTB3 expression is reduced across many tumour types, consistent with a tumour-suppressive role.

description: Late in infection by many enveloped viruses, infected cells fuse with their neighbours to form multinucleated syncytia, and induction of cell-cell fusion describes the machinery that drives this. The same proteins that mediate viral entry act here in reverse geometry: spike protein displayed on an infected cell engages ACE2 on a neighbour, forming synapse-like contacts that mature into a fusion pore. Proteolytic priming sets the probability of fusion, with the transmembrane serine protease TMPRSS2 and the proprotein convertase FURIN cleaving spike into its S1 and S2 fragments. Fusion also requires remodelling of the target membrane's lipid asymmetry, supplied by the anoctamin family: calcium-activated scramblases such as TMEM16F expose phosphatidylserine, while related members act as calcium-gated chloride channels. Syncytia are prominent in pneumocytes in severe COVID-19, shelter replication from immune detection, and can engulf lymphocytes, linking this fusion to lymphopenia and lung pathology.

description: Adipogenesis is the developmental route by which precursor cells become fat cells, the units of adipose tissue that buffer the body's energy supply and, in their brown and beige forms, burn substrate to generate heat. Its output determines how much lipid can be stored safely, how much leptin and adiponectin circulate, and how well insulin-stimulated glucose uptake works; when the programme fails or is overloaded, the result is lipodystrophy at one extreme and insulin-resistant obesity at the other. The nuclear receptor PPARG with RXRA, together with the C/EBP factors, drives the terminal gene programme, and their transcriptional output depends on Mediator subunits, p300/CBP and NCOA coactivators being exchanged for NCoR/SMRT-HDAC and NuRD repressor complexes. Thermogenic identity adds PRDM16, EBF2 and PGC-1 coactivators driving UCP1 and mitochondrial genes, while Wnt ligands and TNF/NF-\u03baB signalling restrain differentiation. Mature output includes FABP4, PLIN1, LPL, CD36 and GLUT4.

description: Cells constantly read the physical forces around them — blood flow shear, tissue stiffness, stretch, compression, touch — and cellular responses to mechanical stimuli are how those forces become chemical signals. This is what lets endothelium adjust vessel tone and remodel to laminar versus turbulent flow, bone cells sense load, and sensory structures register touch; its failure contributes to atherosclerosis at sites of disturbed flow, hypertension and disuse bone loss. Force is detected by mechanically gated cation channels such as PIEZO1 and TRPV4, by integrins linked through talin and vinculin to the actin cytoskeleton and fibronectin-rich matrix, and by junctional and G protein-coupled sensors including PECAM1 and VE-cadherin. Downstream, calcium entry, adhesion kinases, PI3K–AKT and mTOR complexes, adenylate cyclase–PKA signalling, ATP release through pannexin to purinergic receptors, nitric oxide production by endothelial NOS, and NF-kB and YAP1 translate force into altered gene expression, growth and cell behaviour.

description: Dengue virus depends on a large set of host proteins to replicate, and the same interactions drive the vascular leak and inflammation of severe dengue. This map of dengue virus-host interactions collects the cellular machinery the virus co-opts or subverts: heparan sulfate proteoglycans such as syndecans and glypicans that serve as attachment factors, the innate sensing and interferon arm built around MDA5, MAVS, STING, TRIM25 and STAT2 that the virus antagonises, and complement components and regulators that secreted NS1 engages in the bloodstream. Nuclear localisation of viral capsid and NS5 places them alongside RNA polymerase II, spliceosomal snRNPs and SR/hnRNP proteins, and the cleavage-polyadenylation machinery, so host mRNA processing is remodelled during infection. Autophagy initiation, mTOR complexes and fatty acid synthesis supply membranes and lipids, while junctional proteins such as ZO-1 link these events to endothelial barrier failure and hemorrhagic disease.

description: Affinity selection of immunoglobulins is the quality-control step of the germinal centre reaction: B cells that have mutated their antibody genes are tested for how well the product binds antigen, and only the best binders survive. This is what turns a first, weak antibody response into high-affinity protective immunity and long-lived memory; its failure gives immunodeficiency, while its misfiring underlies autoantibody production and the lymphomas that arise from germinal centre B cells. Antigen is displayed as immune complexes held by follicular dendritic cells through complement receptors CR1 and CR2 and the Fc receptor FCGR2B; high-affinity B cells extract it using non-muscle myosin IIA force, degrade it via cathepsins and present peptides on MHC class II to follicular helper T cells, which supply CD40 ligand, IL4 and IL21 as survival signals. Cells then re-enter cycles of AICDA-initiated hypermutation resolved by uracil excision, mismatch repair and error-prone polymerases, under BCL6-dominated transcription.
